title: From an encounter to a claim.
intro: Keep the room, its record and our interpretation within reach of one another. These questions return through the existing spine; they do not add a new tutorial subject to every hall.

steps.title: What happened?
steps.text: Begin with the body, object and action. A still capture shows one moment; movement and response need an account through time.

steps.title: What did we keep?
steps.text: Name the recorded values, their units and frame, the sampling rule and any capacity limit. A pause, a missed event and an empty entry are different things.

steps.title: How did we arrange it?
steps.text: Name the operation: reorder, transform, round, filter, average or count. Keep the earlier record available when the purpose is to compare representations.

steps.title: What can we claim?
steps.text: Follow the result back to its evidence. Separate an observed event, a declared dependency, a measured similarity and an artistic interpretation.

returns.question: What disappears between retained positions?
returns.text: The movement gate can keep a pause out of the list. Read the rule beside the line it produces.

returns.question: What changes when the same trace becomes a sculpture?
returns.text: Compare the received positions with their recentered, scaled and rounded displays. The event and its later uses remain distinct.

returns.question: What counts as one entry?
returns.text: Follow the planned distinction between an address and what occupies it. Changing order changes the arrangement we encounter.

returns.question: What does one colour value describe?
returns.text: A stored value and its appearance in a lit room differ. Replacing that value also differs from recording its history.

returns.question: Did the relations change, or their arrangement?
returns.text: Move a point while preserving adjacency. A different drawing can direct attention without adding a connection.

returns.question: What does this count establish?
returns.text: Read the fictional record behind an arrow before interpreting its prominence. An omitted record and an unrecorded event are different absences.

returns.question: Who defined the permitted pairs?
returns.text: The algorithm solves an allocation within declared relations. Return to those declarations when asking what its result permits or excludes.

categories: Keep the selected hall while switching between Hall images and Relations. In Relations, compare spine order, declared prerequisites and shared artifacts. Each view selects another relation; a shared token does not establish shared live state. Grouping photographs by visual resemblance would be a further proposal, not a verified dependency.
process: For a spring settling or an attachment failing, a useful future record would keep several moments from the same run, with their order and conditions. The current atlas contains saved still captures; it does not yet provide event replay. A photograph from another run cannot silently fill a missing moment.
precision: Automatic capture still has tracking, sampling and coordinate choices. A beautiful diagram, a successful screenshot and a runnable tutorial are different kinds of evidence. None substitutes for the others.

source.title: Lev Manovich — Big Data, Visualization, and Digital Humanities, CUNY syllabus (2013)
source.note: Our adaptation draws on the syllabus's distinctions between artifacts and processes, data and metadata, feature selection and cultural categories. Its software list is historical; it is not our installation guide.
